title: SMS, app code or key: what each one stops
body_md:
## Anything you can read aloud

A friendly voice on the phone says someone is trying to get into your account from abroad, and that cancelling the attempt takes only the six digits that have just arrived on your phone. The digits are genuine. So is the sign-in the caller has open on their own screen, which is waiting for exactly that code.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) asks for more than a password, but its methods are not equals: each stops some attacks and waves others through. So “do I have two steps?” is the wrong question. Ask this: **could someone who knows my password, who has taken over my phone number, or who runs a fake login page still get in?** Choose the strongest method on offer, provided you could get back in after losing your phone. An account left on a password alone while you wait for the perfect option is usually worse off.

### What each method stops, and what it lets through

**SMS or voice codes** get in the way of a stolen or reused password. Two things can go wrong. The number can be taken over in a SIM swap, where a scammer talks the carrier into moving it onto a SIM they hold, and the code can be coaxed out of you by phone or typed into a fake page. If SMS is all a service offers, it still beats nothing. Ask your carrier about an account PIN or protection against number transfers.

**Authenticator-app codes (TOTP, time-based one-time passwords)** are worked out on your device from a secret shared with the service at setup. Depending on its settings, the app may store or sync that secret, so “it lives only on this phone” is not safe to assume. A number thief gets nothing here. But you still type the code by hand, and a phishing page can pass it to the real site at once. Save the recovery codes, and learn how to move to a new phone before you part with the old one.

**FIDO security keys and passkeys** differ in kind: there is no code to read out. They use a cryptographic credential tied to the domain of the real service, and when WebAuthn is properly implemented a lookalike site cannot collect an answer the real one would accept. A physical key is generally tied to that one device; a passkey may sync or stay put, depending on its provider. All of it rests on the service’s setup, your device and your recovery choices. And a site may keep SMS as a side entrance after you register a key, so read the whole sign-in and recovery settings instead of assuming the strongest factor is the only way in.

Start with your email, your password manager and any account that can reset others. Banks and employers may offer only some of these methods: use the best on offer, ask about alternatives, and keep to workplace policy. If a code arrives that you never asked for, approve nothing and share nothing; open the service yourself and check recent activity. A code goes to no one who phoned you, even a caller who says they are support.

widget_config.goal: Choose and set up a second sign-in step by what it stops against phishing and how you get back in if you lose it, not by a ranking.
widget_config.today_action: Open the security and recovery settings of your main email. Turn on the strongest second step you can also back up, keep the recovery codes somewhere safe, and write down any weaker route that can still get in.
widget_config.scope: A general comparison; the options vary by service, carrier and country. The cases and exercises are invented. NIST is a US federal technical standard. Checked 2026-10-20.

blocks.title: The caller wants your code
blocks.situation: You are halfway through signing in to your email when the phone rings. A calm “support agent” says a sign-in attempt has been spotted, and to cancel it he needs you to read out the new code from your authenticator app.
blocks.analysis: That code is exactly what a live attacker’s login is waiting for, and neither an SMS code nor an app code can tell a real request from one that has been relayed. Hang up, open the service yourself and check recent activity. The code goes to no caller, whoever they say they are.

blocks.title: The bank that only texts
blocks.situation: Your bank protects the account with a password and a code sent by SMS. Its published settings list no authenticator app, no security key and no passkey.
blocks.analysis: A texted code still beats a password alone. Keep it, protect your number with the carrier if it offers a way, and ask the bank whether anything stronger is on the way. Switching off your only second step because it is weaker than a key would leave you less safe, not more.

blocks.title: The inbox your trip depends on
blocks.setup: Four separate mailboxes, all invented, each holding the bookings for an upcoming trip. Each mailbox has its own starting facts, so nothing you choose in one carries into the next.

steps.prompt: Mailbox 1: it offers SMS, authenticator-app codes and FIDO keys. You are on its security page, which you opened from your own bookmark, and no key is registered yet. Which do you set up first to resist phishing?

choices.text: Stay with SMS alone; it is the easiest second step.
choices.consequence: A stolen password no longer works by itself, but a SIM swap or a relayed code still gets through.
choices.explanation: SMS is worth having when it is all you can get, but a stronger factor on offer covers more attacks.

choices.text: Register a FIDO key on the mailbox’s own security page.
choices.consequence: The login is now tied to the real service’s domain, and a lookalike page gets nothing it can use.
choices.explanation: A code you type can be relayed to the real site. A properly configured WebAuthn login cannot be.

steps.prompt: Mailbox 2: this one already has a FIDO key registered, and you own a spare. The service allows a second key and gives out recovery codes. How do you prepare for losing the first key?

choices.text: Register the spare key and keep the recovery codes somewhere protected, apart from the keys.
choices.consequence: Losing the key you carry every day no longer means losing the mailbox.
choices.explanation: Plan the way back in while you still have access, and guard the backups as carefully as the key.

choices.text: Skip the backup; a FIDO key cannot fail.
choices.consequence: If your only key is lost or snapped in half, you are locked out.
choices.explanation: Resistance to phishing does nothing for a lost authenticator.

steps.prompt: Mailbox 3: a FIDO key is registered, yet SMS still works as another way to sign in. What do you do with that fact?

choices.text: Check whether SMS can safely be removed or is needed for recovery, and write down the risk that remains.
choices.consequence: You know which route is now the weakest.
choices.explanation: Registering a key does not retire the older routes by itself.

choices.text: Conclude that the key has made every remaining route resistant to phishing.
choices.consequence: A weaker fallback may still let an attacker in.
choices.explanation: An account is only as strong as the weakest sign-in or recovery route that still works.

steps.prompt: Mailbox 4: MFA is on. A sign-in code you did not request arrives, and a minute later someone phones, says they are from support and asks you to read it out. What do you do?

choices.text: Read the code to the caller.
choices.consequence: They type it into the login they have open, and they are in.
choices.explanation: Real support has no use for your one-time sign-in code.

choices.text: Share and approve nothing. Open the mailbox yourself and check recent activity.
choices.consequence: The attacker’s login stalls without the code.
choices.explanation: An unexpected code means either a slip or someone trying to sign in. Check without using any link from the message.

blocks.debrief: Four separate decisions, one habit: pair the strongest factor an account offers with a backup you can really use, and look at every fallback that still works. If a choice went the other way, go back and run it again before you try this on a real account.

blocks.title: Match the method to the threat

questions.prompt: What does an authenticator app protect against that SMS does not?

choices.text: The risk that whoever takes over your mobile number receives your codes.
choices.explanation: The app makes the code on your device, and nothing is sent to your number.

choices.text: Every phishing page that asks for a code.
choices.explanation: A code typed by hand can be relayed to the real site.

questions.prompt: A site offers only SMS for its second step. What is a sensible move?

choices.text: Leave MFA off until security keys are supported.
choices.explanation: That leaves the account open to anyone who has the password.

choices.text: Turn it on, protect your number with the carrier where you can, and watch for stronger options.
choices.explanation: Even a weaker second step cuts the risk of a password-only login.

questions.prompt: What makes a correctly set up FIDO login resistant to phishing?

choices.text: The key produces a longer code that is harder to type.
choices.explanation: The protection comes from the cryptographic tie to the service; the length of a code has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Its response is tied to the identity of the real service.
choices.explanation: A lookalike site cannot reuse a valid response that was meant for the real one.
